assessment: Soy oil is listed as a source of palmitoylethanolamide in an abstract testing subcutaneous micronized palmitoylethanolamide in Alzheimer-model mice. The meeting bundle contains separate Parkinson abstracts.
Corn oil carried tamoxifen for genetic induction in mice. The experiment changed Calhm2 and did not compare corn oil for depressive symptoms.
Medium-chain triglyceride is a proposed nanocarrier component in a theoretical Huntington disease formulation. There is no coconut oil exposure or Parkinson apathy outcome.
Both rat groups received an intraperitoneal medium-chain triglyceride and DMSO vehicle. The between-group motor and pathology comparison varies rotenone and supplies no isolated coconut oil estimate.
Hydroxytyrosol was an analytical internal standard for dopamine measurement. Cortistatin was the experimental treatment.
Both mouse genotypes received intraperitoneal tamoxifen in corn oil to induce recombination. The experiment changed Bmal1 status and gives no corn oil daytime sleepiness contrast.
Hydroxytyrosol appears in discussion of earlier alpha-synuclein fibril studies. The current cell experiment tested dopamine and grape seed extract nanoparticles.
Discussion cites protection from oleuropein and rutin in an earlier cellular study. This experiment measured cellular stress and degeneration after 6-OHDA, without culinary olive oil.
The oleuropein poster tested neutrophils in vitro for an autoimmune disease hypothesis. Parkinson symptoms occur in other abstracts in the conference bundle.
Alpha-linolenic acid is a pathway label in metabolomic enrichment. The Parkinson cohorts were grouped by motor complications, without assigned or measured flaxseed oil for anxiety or constipation.

The MCT-supplemented Mediterranean diet poster enrolled people with mild cognitive impairment or subjective cognitive decline. Its outcomes were primarily bioimpedance and metabolic measures. Parkinson matches come from the conference bundle.
Alpha-linolenic acid metabolism was a metabolomic pathway in a mouse study of lycopene. There was no flaxseed oil intervention.

Alpha-linolenic acid metabolism appears in pathway enrichment in the metabolomics and Mendelian-randomization analysis. It does not provide a flaxseed oil comparison for rest tremor, rigidity or bradykinesia.

PREDIMED compared Mediterranean diet with extra-virgin olive oil against low-fat advice in adults at high cardiovascular risk. Its outcome was incident depression, without a Parkinson anxiety outcome.
Canola oil was a sham arm and antioxidant vehicle in juvenile rat hydrocephalus. The treatment contrasts concern ventricular and tissue measures rather than Parkinson dyskinesia.

Baseline Parkinson food-frequency analysis reports an olive oil association and an inconclusive safflower oil estimate for total PRO-PD. Neither oil has a constipation-specific estimate or reported grade.

Almond, peanut, grapeseed and linseed oils appear in formulation materials or screening and a medium-chain triglyceride was a candidate surfactant. The rat efficacy formulation used intranasal naringenin nanoemulsion with vitamin E and Capryol 90.
Sesamin is in a cited mouse paper. The current Parkinson rat study manipulated exercise and did not administer sesame oil.
Alpha-linolenic acid appears as a fatty acid abbreviation. The mouse diets varied soybean and coconut-derived fats to study hypothalamic expression, without a flaxseed oil contrast.
Sesamol appears in discussion of a prior rotenone-rat experiment. The current study tested maackiain in worms and cultured cells.
The discussion cites olive-fruit oleuropein derivatives in an earlier aggregation study. Scopoletin was the intervention in the current Parkinson model.
Sesamin is a listed phenolic compound in spice mass spectrometry. No Parkinson participants, sesame oil intervention or depressive symptom outcome was studied.
Plasma alpha-linolenic acid had no clear association with Wexner constipation scores after age or sex adjustment. The study did not compare flaxseed oil intake.
Medium-chain triglyceride occurs in commercial cannabidiol tweets. The social media study does not estimate Parkinson fatigue after coconut oil.
A rehabilitation position paper proposed adding MCT oil and protein to gruel in a drug-induced parkinsonism case. There was no administered coconut-oil comparison or outcome for either claim.
Alpha-linolenic acid was a metabolite in Parkinson model brain profiling. The intervention was the Bai Chan Ting combination, without a flaxseed oil arm.
Alpha-linolenic acid is discussed as an EPA and DHA precursor. The experiment tested EPA and DHA and did not administer flaxseed oil or assess rigidity from it.

Bibliometric review indexes quercetin and sesamin in co-cultures and hydroxytyrosol and oleuropein aglycone in worms. Neither primary experiment tested a culinary oil or either named Parkinson symptom.
Sesamol is listed for gastric mucosal myeloperoxidase in an oxidative-stress review. The referenced work does not test sesame oil for depression in Parkinson disease.
Review cites isolated sesamol with buspirone in a mouse stress-induced anxiety experiment. It does not establish a sesame oil effect or a Parkinson cohort.
Hydroxytyrosol with EPA or DHA appears in cited preclinical fatty liver models. The review does not report olive oil and Parkinson symptom comparisons.
Post-COVID review discusses olive fruit and leaf oleuropein as a potential treatment for renal inflammation. No clinical olive oil Parkinson comparison was reported.
Review identifies flaxseed as a dietary source of alpha-linolenic acid in a discussion of COPD cognition. No flaxseed oil anxiety result in Parkinson disease was reported.
Review cites sesamol in diabetes-associated rat cognitive impairment. The endpoint and exposure differ from sesame oil and depressive symptoms in Parkinson disease.
Hydroxytyrosol is one antioxidant listed in an arsenic toxicity review. The source does not test olive oil for anxiety in Parkinson disease.

The review summarizes separately administered sesamol and naringenin in a rotenone rat experiment. The traced primary report is a constituent study and gives no sesame oil anxiety or depression contrast.
The sesamol discussion traces to the 2013 rat study of motor and dopaminergic measures. The intervention was isolated sesamol, without a sesame oil arm or a Parkinson patient anxiety outcome.
The cited sesamol solid lipid nanoparticles were tested in an intracerebroventricular streptozotocin cognitive-impairment model. The review does not report the sesame oil claims.
Review discusses hydroxytyrosol metabolite effects on alpha-synuclein fibril formation in a prior co-incubation study. No culinary oil exposure or symptom outcome was assessed.
Alpha-linolenic acid was a search term. The 23 included trials tested EPA and/or DHA, including three Parkinson trials. The review supplies no flaxseed oil anxiety or pain comparison.

The olive oil mention is one component of the cited five-week Mediterranean diet in Parkinson constipation. Both chows in the traced ketogenic animal study contained coconut oil, and the study did not report dyskinesia.
Rapeseed oil is named as a dietary alpha-linolenic acid source in the omega-3 gut-brain review. No intervention assigns canola oil or measures the matched Parkinson symptom.
Review cites sesamol in manganese-induced neuroinflammation and cognitive impairment. The cited exposure is an isolated compound in an animal toxicant model.
The oleuropein entry concerns 6-OHDA-exposed PC12 cell viability and apoptosis. The structure-activity review has no original olive oil symptom outcome.
Review cites serum alpha-linolenic acid measurements in a dopaminergic-disease metabolomics comparison. Serum concentrations are not a test of flaxseed oil or a symptom-specific treatment response.
The cited MPTP experiment compared two mouse diets containing different quantities of coconut oil and other macronutrients. It measured motor assays, without an isolated coconut oil fatigue contrast.

Review describes oleuropein carried in mesenchymal-cell-derived extracellular vesicle hybrids for alpha-synuclein aggregation assays. The cited intervention and endpoints do not match culinary olive oil.
Alpha-linolenic acid appears in prior work on butyrylcholinesterase expression and lipid homeostasis. No flaxseed oil anxiety or pain comparison is given.

The review identifies NCT05469997. The later reports of this crossover compare Mediterranean-based diets including coconut-derived MCT oil, with bowel and fatigue outcomes but no isolated culinary oil effect.
Review names Miglyol 812N, a triglyceride vehicle in an experimental rotenone model. The route and experimental purpose differ from coconut oil consumption and the four clinical endpoints.

The review combines whole ketogenic diets, ketone products, and medium-chain triglyceride protocols. The cited Parkinson feeding study is the already cataloged Choi comparison, which does not isolate culinary coconut oil.
Rapeseed oil appears in a table of alpha-linolenic acid content. The narrative prevention review gives no assigned canola oil comparison on either symptom.
Review cites a manganese rat experiment testing isolated sesamol and thymol and inflammatory signaling. It provides no culinary sesame oil pain or motor symptom estimate.
Rapeseed oil is mentioned in a cross-sectional dietary-pattern study of older adults at metabolic risk. The cited cognitive outcomes are outside the Parkinson claim.
Alpha-linolenic acid is discussed as a fatty acid influencing cardiolipin remodeling. The review provides no flaxseed oil treatment or rigidity and bradykinesia estimates.

Review discusses isolated hydroxytyrosol, oleuropein and derivatives in aggregation models and cites the already screened rotenone mouse oleuropein experiment. No original olive oil clinical symptom result was reported.
Bibliometric review indexes sesamol in Alzheimer-model mice and sesamin combined with astaxanthin in mild cognitive impairment. It provides no sesame oil Parkinson depression comparison.
Rapeseed oil was a gavage vehicle control in a cited developmental chlorpyrifos rat experiment. The reported comparison varied pesticide exposure and measured ileal endpoints.
The review table pairs medium-chain triglycerides with Alzheimer and epilepsy metabolic interventions. No coconut oil result on the matched Parkinson symptom appears there.
Review cites astaxanthin plus sesamin capsules in mild cognitive impairment. Processing-speed and cognitive outcomes do not provide a sesame oil Parkinson depression estimate.
Review describes a high-fat fruit-fly screen of several dietary fats including linseed oil. It does not give a flaxseed oil pain comparison in Parkinson disease.
Olive oil is a binder matrix for an experimental gastrointestinal glucose sensor. The paper does not estimate anxiety after olive oil ingestion.
The cited sesamol study used APP/PS1 Alzheimer-model mice and inflammatory or microbiota measures. It provides no sesame oil anxiety or depression comparison in Parkinson disease.
The cited ketogenic and medium-chain triglyceride experiment used transgenic Alzheimer mice. This review gives no coconut oil comparison for the matched Parkinson endpoint.
Alpha-linolenic acid is introduced as one omega-3 fatty acid in a pathogenesis review. The discussion provides no isolated flaxseed oil symptom result.

Review traces to the KIM and Choi broader MCT-diet trials and a flaxseed-derived omega-3 plus vitamin E trial. Those comparisons do not isolate culinary coconut oil or flaxseed oil for the named endpoints.
Hydroxytyrosol appears in a table of epigenetic interventions for an experimental Alzheimer model. Anxiety-like behavior in that setting does not establish olive oil effects in Parkinson disease.
The medium-chain triglyceride references concern ketogenic regimens in cancer. The Parkinson diet discussion gives no coconut oil result on the matched symptom.
The review discusses flax oil with vitamin C in attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder. It does not test the three Parkinson symptom claims.
Sunflower oil is listed as a dietary tocotrienol source. The review does not report a sunflower oil intervention on the matched Parkinson outcome.
Sesamol appears in a cited comparison of antioxidant properties of commercial phytochemical preparations. There was no Parkinson patient sesame oil pain trial.
Sesamin is listed in an MPP+-exposed neuronal and glial co-culture study. The review gives no sesame oil intervention or symptom-level clinical result.
Oleuropein is one compound listed as potentially neuroprotective in a pharmacogenomics review. There is no original culinary olive oil intervention or symptom estimate.
Alpha-linolenic acid is discussed as an essential precursor in fatty acid metabolism. The general nutrition review does not estimate flaxseed oil effects on the four Parkinson symptoms.
Review cites a flaxseed oil experiment on arsenic-induced cardiotoxicity in rats. It does not provide a Parkinson pain estimate.
The review contrasts DHA and alpha-linolenic acid effects in preclinical serotonergic work. It does not test culinary flaxseed oil or the two matched Parkinson symptoms.
Review traces to the rotenone-rat study testing isolated sesamol and naringenin separately. It reports motor coordination proxies, without a culinary sesame oil Parkinson anxiety comparison.
Review traces to a mouse study feeding whole sesame seed oil before a 6-OHDA lesion. The primary report describes tissue endpoints and gives no oil grade, depressive symptom or human motor outcome.
Medium-chain triglycerides are mentioned as alternative energy substrates for the brain. The nutrition review does not test coconut oil for the three Parkinson symptoms.
Alpha-linolenic acid is listed with other nutrients in marine nutraceuticals. The review gives no flaxseed oil Parkinson anxiety or pain comparison.
Sesamin is listed as a lignan with potential PPAR-alpha activity. The review provides no sesame oil Parkinson anxiety or depression outcome.
Alpha-linolenic acid appears in a cited purslane study of inflammatory markers in sensitized rats. No flaxseed oil Parkinson anxiety or pain comparison was reported.
Medium-chain triglycerides dissolved coenzyme Q10 for an experimental oleogel. This formulation example does not provide a coconut oil Parkinson fatigue outcome.
Soy oil is named as a dietary source of coenzyme Q10. The review does not provide an intervention testing refined soybean oil for Parkinson rest tremor.
The review lists alpha-linolenic acid as a dietary fatty acid and cites a Parkinson omega-3 plus vitamin E trial using total UPDRS. It does not isolate flaxseed oil or the six listed symptoms.
Oleuropein is listed with compounds studied in protein misfolding models. The EGCG review supplies no culinary olive oil comparison or original Parkinson symptom result.
Medium-chain triglyceride oil appears in recommendations for pediatric lipid myopathy. The review does not provide a coconut oil intervention for the three Parkinson outcomes.
Alpha-linolenic acid is a precursor in an oxylipin pathway figure for pulmonary inflammation. There is no flaxseed oil Parkinson pain comparison.
Alpha-linolenic acid plus quercetin is cited for cardiovascular markers in adults without the target diagnosis. This is not an isolated flaxseed oil comparison on Parkinson symptoms.

The cited Fujikawa rat study used isolated sesamin and a separate botanical extract, with water and olive oil as vehicle control. Pole and catalepsy assays do not supply a clinical depressive symptom or sesame oil effect.

MCT oil was proposed as a way to make ketogenic protocols more tolerable. The discussed clinical comparisons concern whole diets or exogenous ketones, without a coconut oil effect on the named symptoms.
Linseed oil is discussed as an alpha-linolenic acid source and in a prior rat inflammatory-marker study. No isolated flaxseed oil estimate on Parkinson anxiety appears in the review.

The review suggests a depression benefit from cited sesamin studies. The 2017 primary abstract reports narrow-beam motor balance and tissue outcomes in 6-OHDA rats, without a depression or whole sesame oil comparison.
Alpha-linolenic acid and ALA-rich oils appear in an Alzheimer oxylipin review, including vascular and cognitive model citations. There is no flaxseed oil Parkinson symptom estimate.
The cited MCT ketogenic interventions concern epilepsy or Alzheimer disease. The Parkinson diet discussion does not isolate coconut oil or report a coconut oil fatigue outcome.

The Mediterranean diet review describes plant-derived alpha-linolenic acid as a polyunsaturated fatty acid. This passage gives no original flaxseed oil outcomes for the five matched Parkinson symptoms.
A participant who withdrew from the ketogenic period reported longer OFF time after a high-fat meal. The report gives no refined coconut oil exposure, drug concentration or controlled estimate.
Apathy is described as an existing barrier to preparing food and tracking adherence. No apathy change estimate is given after MCT or virgin coconut oil.
